body:
Arrival and purpose of the Cabinet Mission

In 1946, the British Labour government sent a Cabinet Mission to India to negotiate the constitutional framework for transferring power. Its 3 members were Lord Pethick-Lawrence, the Secretary of State for India, Sir Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander.

The Mission sought an arrangement acceptable to the Congress and Muslim League. The Congress generally favoured a united India with an effective central government, while the Muslim League demanded political arrangements capable of protecting Muslim-majority regions and pursued the demand for Pakistan.

On 16 May 1946, the Mission announced a constitutional plan. It rejected the proposal to establish completely separate sovereign states at that stage and instead recommended a Union of India with a narrowly defined central authority.

A Union with limited central subjects

Under the proposed Constitution, the Union would include British India and the princely states. The Union government would control only the following principal subjects:

  • Foreign affairs, concerning India's relations with other countries.
  • Defence, concerning national military responsibilities.
  • Communications, concerning specified common communication systems.

The Union would also have the authority needed to raise finances for these responsibilities.

All other subjects and residuary powers were to belong to the provinces. Princely states would retain the powers they had not ceded to the Union.

Thus, the Mission proposed a much more limited Centre than a government holding general powers over all subjects.

Provincial groups

The Mission proposed that provinces could form groups with common executives and legislatures for subjects they agreed to administer jointly. These groups would operate within the broader proposed Union.

For the initial constitution-making process, the provincial representatives were arranged into 3 sections: A, B and C.

SectionProvincesGeneral description
AMadras, Bombay, United Provinces, Bihar, Central Provinces and OrissaPredominantly Hindu-majority provinces
BPunjab, North-West Frontier Province and SindNorth-western provinces
CBengal and AssamEastern provinces

The sections were intended to discuss provincial constitutions and determine whether group constitutions should be established. Representatives would then participate in framing the Union Constitution.

Were the groups compulsory?

The distinction between an initial section and a permanent group became a major source of disagreement.

The Mission's procedure required provincial representatives to meet in their designated sections during the initial constitution-making process. It also provided a later opportunity for a province to leave a group through a vote of its legislature after the first general election under the new Constitution.

The Congress argued that provinces should be free to choose whether to participate in grouping. The Muslim League regarded compulsory initial grouping as essential to protecting the political position of Muslim-majority provinces.

The Cabinet Mission did not propose 3 independent countries. Sections A, B and C were part of a scheme for a proposed Union. The disagreement concerned the degree to which provinces were obliged to enter the initial sections and could later leave groups.

Communal safeguards

The proposed Union would have a legislature and executive containing representatives of British India and the princely states. For major communal questions, the Mission proposed a special voting safeguard: a decision would require a majority of all members present and voting and also a majority of the representatives present and voting from each of the 2 major communities, Hindus and Muslims.

This was intended to prevent important communal decisions from being determined solely by an overall numerical majority.

Review of constitutional arrangements

The proposed constitutional structure also allowed a provincial legislative assembly, by a majority vote, to seek reconsideration of constitutional terms after an initial period of 10 years, with further opportunities at 10-year intervals.

Prelims focus

  • Cabinet Mission members: Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps and A. V. Alexander.
  • Main statement: 16 May 1946.
  • Union subjects: Foreign affairs, defence and communications, with necessary financing powers.
  • Residuary powers: Proposed for provinces, unlike the 1935 Act's discretionary arrangement.
  • Initial provincial sections: A, B and C.
  • Grouping dispute: Initial section membership versus later freedom to leave a group.
  • Trap: The Cabinet Mission Plan sought a united constitutional arrangement; it did not itself establish Pakistan.

[British Parliament, House of Lords, India: Statement by the Cabinet Mission, 16 May 1946, paragraphs 15–19; British Parliament, House of Commons, India (Cabinet Mission), 18 July 1946, explanation of initial sections and the later right to leave groups; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Chapter 14, Understanding Partition, section on the Cabinet Mission; parliamentary records consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946: A United India with a Limited Centre and Provincial Groups

body:
How the Cabinet Mission proposed to form a Constituent Assembly

The Cabinet Mission also proposed machinery for framing a new Indian Constitution. It recognised that an election based on universal adult franchise would take considerable time. Instead, it recommended using the existing provincial legislatures to select representatives indirectly.

The original scheme provided for a Constituent Assembly of 389 members, subject to arrangements for princely state representation.

Source of representationSeats
Governors' Provinces292
Chief Commissioners' Provinces4
Princely states93
Total proposed strength389

The 4 Chief Commissioners' Provinces included in the allocation were Delhi, Ajmer-Merwara, Coorg and British Baluchistan. The total allocation for British India was therefore 296 seats, with the remaining 93 seats allotted to the princely states.

Provincial representation was calculated broadly on the basis of population, approximately 1 seat for every 1 million people. The main electoral categories recognised for provincial representation were General, Muslim and Sikh.

Method of selecting representatives

Within provincial legislative assemblies, members of each recognised community elected the allotted Constituent Assembly members for that community. The prescribed method was proportional representation by the single transferable vote.

In this method, electors rank candidates by preference, and surplus votes of elected candidates and votes of eliminated candidates may be transferred to continuing candidates according to the next available preferences. It differs from a simple system in which each elector chooses only 1 candidate and the candidate with the most votes wins.

Representatives of princely states were to be selected through arrangements determined by consultation with the states. Their participation was not based on a general election conducted throughout the princely states.

The Constituent Assembly was not elected by universal adult franchise. Its provincial members were chosen indirectly through provincial legislatures. The figure of 389 refers to the original pre-Partition scheme, not the later strength of the Assembly for independent India.

Congress and Muslim League disagreement

The Cabinet Mission's proposals initially created some possibility of agreement. However, the Congress and Muslim League disagreed over the meaning and compulsory character of provincial grouping.

The Congress maintained that provinces should retain meaningful freedom concerning group membership. The Muslim League insisted that the initial grouping arrangements were an essential part of the settlement.

The League ultimately withdrew its acceptance of the plan in July 1946 and called for political mobilisation in support of its Pakistan demand.

Direct Action Day, 16 August 1946

The Muslim League designated 16 August 1946 as Direct Action Day. Severe communal violence broke out in Calcutta and continued for several days. Communal tensions and violence subsequently affected other regions as well.

These developments made negotiations increasingly difficult and weakened the prospects of implementing the Cabinet Mission's united constitutional framework.

Formation of the Interim Government

An Interim Government began functioning on 2 September 1946, with Jawaharlal Nehru serving as Vice-President of the Viceroy's Executive Council.

The Interim Government was a transitional executive operating before independence. It was not the same institution as the Constituent Assembly, whose principal task was constitution-making.

The Muslim League did not join the Interim Government at its formation but entered it in October 1946. Political disagreement between the major parties nevertheless continued.

First meeting of the Constituent Assembly

The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946 in New Delhi. The Muslim League boycotted its proceedings.

The Assembly's work therefore began without participation from one of the principal parties in the negotiations. Following Partition, the membership of the Constituent Assembly for India was reduced to 299.

Three different institutions

  • Cabinet Mission: The British delegation that negotiated and proposed constitutional arrangements.
  • Interim Government: The transitional executive that began functioning on 2 September 1946.
  • Constituent Assembly: The body that first met on 9 December 1946 to prepare India's Constitution.

These institutions were connected in the same political transition but performed different functions.

Prelims focus

  • Original proposed Assembly strength: 389 members.
  • Seat allocation: 292 Governors' Provinces, 4 Chief Commissioners' Provinces and 93 princely states.
  • Selection method: Indirect election through provincial legislatures using proportional representation by single transferable vote.
  • Direct Action Day: 16 August 1946.
  • Interim Government: Formed on 2 September 1946.
  • First Constituent Assembly meeting: 9 December 1946.
  • Trap: The original figure of 389 should not be confused with the post-Partition strength of 299.

[British Parliament, House of Lords, India: Statement by the Cabinet Mission, 16 May 1946, paragraphs 18–20, particularly the allocation of seats and election procedure; NCERT, Indian Constitution at Work, Class 11, Chapter 1, pp. 15–16; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 125–126; Selected Works of Jawaharlal Nehru, Second Series, Volume 1, editorial note on the Interim Government of 1946, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The proposed 389 seats comprised 296 from British India and 93 from princely states; provincial legislatures elected provincial members indirectly.
pictures.caption: The composition and indirect election of the Constituent Assembly originally proposed in 1946.

title: The Constituent Assembly Proposal, 1946: Representation, Elections and Political Deadlock

body:
Why the Cabinet Mission settlement could not be implemented

The Cabinet Mission Plan attempted to preserve Indian unity through a limited Union and provincial groups. Its implementation depended on agreement between the Congress, Muslim League and other political interests.

Disagreement over grouping, the League's withdrawal from the proposed settlement, the boycott of the Constituent Assembly and worsening communal violence prevented the plan from producing an agreed constitutional framework for undivided India.

The British government then moved towards a definite timetable for transferring power.

Attlee's announcement of 20 February 1947

On 20 February 1947, British Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced that the British government intended to transfer power into Indian hands not later than June 1948.

This was a deadline for completing the transfer, not the date on which independence eventually occurred.

Attlee also announced the replacement of Lord Wavell by Lord Mountbatten as Viceroy. Mountbatten assumed office in March 1947 and was charged with overseeing the final transfer of power.

The 3 June Plan

As agreement on an undivided constitutional settlement became increasingly unlikely, Mountbatten consulted Indian political leaders. The British government announced a new transfer-of-power plan on 3 June 1947, commonly called the Mountbatten Plan or 3 June Plan.

Unlike the Cabinet Mission's proposal for a united India, the June plan accepted the possibility of partition and the establishment of separate successor authorities.

It provided procedures for determining the future of provinces affected by partition, including Punjab and Bengal, and paved the way for the creation of the Dominions of India and Pakistan.

Cabinet Mission Plan, 16 May 1946: Proposed a united India with a limited Centre and provincial groups.
3 June Plan, 1947: Provided the political basis for transfer of power with Partition.

Indian Independence Act, 1947

The British Parliament passed the Indian Independence Act, 1947, which received royal assent on 18 July 1947.

Section 1 of the Act provided that, from 15 August 1947, 2 independent Dominions would be established: India and Pakistan.

Principal legal consequences

  • End of British rule: Authority was transferred to the new Dominions from the appointed day, 15 August 1947.
  • Partition: The Act made arrangements for the partition of Punjab and Bengal and the territories of the 2 Dominions.
  • Legislative authority: The new Dominions received authority to make their own laws. Acts subsequently passed by the British Parliament would not automatically apply to them.
  • Constitution-making: The Constituent Assembly of each Dominion could exercise legislative and constitution-making powers under the new arrangements.
  • Princely states: British paramountcy over Indian princely states lapsed. The Crown's former paramountcy was not automatically transferred to either Dominion.

Dominion status and constitutional independence

The 1947 Act established independent Dominions, not republics. During the transitional period, the 1935 constitutional framework continued in an adapted form until new constitutional arrangements could replace it.

The distinction is important: 15 August 1947 marks independence from British rule under the Indian Independence Act. It should not be confused with the date of the Government of India Act, 1935, or with the later commencement of India's republican Constitution.

Final comparison of the principal constitutional measures

YearMeasureCore distinction
1909Indian Councils ActExpanded councils and introduced separate Muslim electorates
1919Government of India ActIntroduced provincial dyarchy and a bicameral Central Legislature
1935Government of India ActIntroduced provincial autonomy; proposed a federation that never operated
1942Cripps proposalsOffered a post-war Dominion and a provincial opt-out provision
1945Wavell PlanSought reconstitution of the existing Executive Council
1946Cabinet Mission PlanProposed a united Union and constitution-making machinery
1947Indian Independence ActEstablished the independent Dominions of India and Pakistan

How to distinguish proposals from results

The principal constitutional changes did not all have the same legal status. The 1909 and 1919 Acts expanded or reorganised institutions within British rule. The 1935 Act introduced provincial autonomy but failed to bring its proposed federation into operation. The 1942 Cripps proposals were not accepted. The 1945 Wavell negotiations failed. The 1946 Cabinet Mission produced constitution-making arrangements but not an agreed constitution for undivided India. The 1947 Indian Independence Act finally established the legal framework for transfer of power.

When comparing these measures, identify whether the question concerns legislative representation, responsibility of ministers, division of governmental powers, constitution-making or actual independence. These are related but distinct stages of constitutional development.

Prelims focus

  • 20 February 1947: Attlee announced transfer of power not later than June 1948.
  • 3 June 1947: Mountbatten Plan accepted a partition-based transfer of power.
  • 18 July 1947: Indian Independence Act received royal assent.
  • 15 August 1947: The Act established 2 independent Dominions.
  • Princely states: British paramountcy lapsed rather than passing automatically to the new Dominions.
  • Trap: The Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 and the Mountbatten Plan of 1947 proposed different political outcomes.

[British Parliament, Hansard, Indian Policy, 20 February 1947, announcement of the transfer deadline; British Parliament, House of Commons, India (Transfer of Power), 3 June 1947, announcement of the Partition plan; Indian Independence Act, 1947, as enacted on 18 July 1947, particularly sections 1, 2–7 and 8; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 125–127; NCERT, Indian Constitution at Work, Class 11, Chapter 1, pp. 15–16. Parliamentary and legislative records consulted 22 November 2026.]
